author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Ape Escape 2: operating gadgets with the right analog stick
summary: The left analog stick moves the character and the right operates gadgets. Preserving that control scheme is essential when revisiting the game.
heroAlt: A real DualShock 2 controller showing the two analog sticks used for movement and gadgets in Ape Escape 2

sourceLabels.game-reference: Ape Escape 2 control and release reference

blocks.text: Give each analog stick a different job

Ape Escape 2 arrived in Japan in 2002, with releases in other regions afterward. The left analog stick moved the character, while the right analog stick operated the selected gadget. The buttons on the upper edge and front of the controller supported this arrangement. Players accustomed to right-stick camera control had to learn a different control scheme.
Select a gadget, then operate it

Selecting a gadget prepared an action; moving the right analog stick performed it. A net or club could therefore respond to a direction relative to the character and target. Successful use depended on tool choice, position and stick movement together. Pressing a single action button did not describe the whole interaction.
Use different tools for different situations

The sequel added gadgets including the Bananarang, Water Cannon and Electro Magnet. Their purposes encouraged players to examine a situation before acting. Distracting a monkey, dealing with a fire and using a magnetic surface required different tools. The level design could test both selecting the appropriate gadget and controlling it correctly.
A companion helped during the adventure

Pipotchi accompanied the main character and provided assistance. This added another source of help in a game that asked players to coordinate movement, selection and directional gadget input. The character and presentation supported the learning process, though they did not remove the need to practice the unusual controls.
Preserve the analog controls during emulation

Correct assignment of the right analog stick remains important when revisiting the game. Replacing analog input with digital directions, or mapping the stick only as a camera control, changes gadget behavior. Correct graphics cannot compensate for incorrectly assigned axes. Ape Escape 2 demonstrates why preserving controller behavior is part of preserving a game’s design.
